chapter: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
title: The Verve date when Ben Webster called for Coleman Hawkins and Budd Johnson
summary: At a Norman Granz session with Ray Brown, Jo Jones and Roy Eldridge, Webster brought in Hawkins and Budd Johnson, whose banter about Ellington was taped.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: At one record date, I think we talked about it, I don't know.
I think that was one on the tape where the sound level was off, so tell me about that record date again.

That's the one. I think Ray Brown was playing bass, I was playing piano. Jo Jones was playing drums. Roy Eldridge was playing trumpet, and that's the one where Ben Webster called up Norman Granz. We'd had a record date the day before. He called him up, he says, "Can you find the old man for me?" He's talking about Coleman Hawkins now.

Now, Ben loved Hawk, just like he was his father, and he said, "Can we book a date for tomorrow?" Norman said, "Yes." And we went up to 50th and Broadway and Ben went to the phone booth and called Budd Johnson. He says, "I think I'm going to rock the boat a little bit and bring Budd in." And you should have heard the -- I guess Norman still has
those tapes. The conversation on there was tremendous.
Norman taped what went on between takes?

And -- what's his name -- Ben would say something to Roy, and talking about Ellington, you know, and Ben was working with Duke, and he said, "You never did make the band." Ben turned to Roy and said, "Man, you couldn't make the band." And Roy said, "Not for the money you was getting, wasn't going to try to make that band." Because Duke wasn't paying anybody anything, you know. And Coleman Hawkins was always shaving his reed. He wouldn't get into the kidding thing, you know.
And Bud Johnson was just as quiet. He'd put his horn to his mouth, but he made everybody play. Because Bud Johnson is a great player, too.

And all we did was just laugh. Ray Brown and the rhythm section just broke up laughing, because we never did get into that conversation. We couldn't. We didn't have the background to get into that, you know?
You said they were what, reminiscing as far back as McKinney's Cotton Pickers --
And you said it was like jazz history.
Oh, I'm glad Norman taped it. I wonder what he's going to do with it.
